customer_name: UK Department of Health & Social Care
business_problem: DHSC needed to scale AI securely across a major public-sector organization so staff could analyze large volumes of health data, accelerate policy work, and support the UK's 10-year health plan without adding friction to critical services.
solution_summary: UK Department of Health & Social Care worked with DXC to operationalize AI as a department-wide productivity and analysis capability rather than leaving it as a pilot. The program moved from user research through design, testing, and deployment in three months, scaling to 4,000 users across policy and operations teams. Staff use AI to analyze large health-related datasets, accelerate policy creation, produce briefings, and speed responses to Parliament, while DXC supports the operating model needed to align policy, delivery, and security at scale. Rather than naming a specific product stack, the story emphasizes co-creation, blended teams, rapid deployment, and day-to-day adoption across a public-sector department. The result is a production AI workflow embedded in knowledge work, turning large data volumes into faster decisions and document outputs that support the UK's 10-year health plan and reduce pressure on the National Health Service.
data_flow: Department teams work against large health and policy datasets, use AI to analyze information and draft policies, briefings, and responses, then feed those outputs into faster decision-making across the department and health-plan delivery workflows.
business_outcome: DHSC reports faster policy creation, quicker responses to Parliament, broader AI-enabled productivity across the department, and a scalable operating model that supports national health-service transformation work.
metrics: 70% of the department now use AI daily
architecture_clues: The rollout moved from user research through design, test, and deployment in three months.
The operating model is described as co-creation with blended teams and a focus on secure scale.
The AI workflow is used against large national-health and policy data volumes to support policy, briefing, and response work.
